subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word or two respecting the visit, just concluding, of the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Japan. As hon. members are aware, we have had the pleasure during the last two days of a visit by the Prime Minister of Japan, Mr. Kishi, who is accompanied by his foreign minister, Mr. Fujiyama.
I regret that owing to pressures on his time which hon. members can appreciate since Mr. Kishi must return for the reopening of the Japanese Diet on January 28, the Prime Minister is unable to spend longer with us. I am pleased to report to the house, however, that in the short space of time available I, together with my colleagues the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), have had most satisfactory exchanges of views with our Japanese guests on the international situation, trade relations between Canada and Japan and other subjects of mutual interest. I may say in all sincerity that the cordiality and frankness which characterized these exchanges were a gratifying testimonial to the friendly relations and confidence existing between Canada and Japan.
Our conversations covered such questions as the importance to both our countries of continued co-operation within the United Nations and the prospects afforded by the forthcoming east-west meeting of heads of states for the alleviation of world tensions, particularly for some progress on the all-important questions of controlled disarmament and the cessation of nuclear tests. In this connection I might note that we are both agreed that exchanges of visits between national leaders can make a significant contribution to increasing the area of confidence that must necessarily precede any durable improvement in international relations.
Discussing the mutual concern of Canada and Japan with the problem of aid to underdeveloped countries, we also found ourselves in complete agreement on the importance of the Colombo plan, not only for improving
the conditions of life and future prospects of the recipient countries but also for improving general relations through the exchanges of students and technicians.
The discussions of economic questions were particularly useful. We reviewed trade matters of general interest, including the important developments which have been taking place in western Europe.
Ministers of both countries noted with satisfaction the progress that had been achieved in developing trade in both directions under our trade agreement. We emphasized the importance we attach to the Japanese market for wheat and for a number of other products. Canadian ministers drew attention to problems of particular difficulty for Canadian industry arising out of rapid increases in imports from Japan which have been highly concentrated in certain lines. It was agreed that solutions for these problems should be sought as quickly as possible.
In conclusion I should like to let the house know that Mr. Kishi has invited me to make a return visit to Japan. In expressing my warm appreciation of this invitation I informed the Japanese Prime Minister that I sincerely hoped such a visit would be possible at a time convenient both to Mr. Kishi and myself.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members of the house will have heard with pleasure that the very welcome visit to Ottawa which we recognized in the house yesterday, of the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Japan was such a satisfactory one. I am sure it will make a contribution to the development and strengthening of the political and economic co-operation which has existed between the two countries at the United Nations, the Colombo plan meetings and elsewhere.
It was an unhappy coincidence that this visit should have coincided with the tragic death of a Canadian who himself, as the ambassador of Canada to Japan, had done so much in strengthening those ties. I am referring, of course, to Mr. Tommy Davis. This visit has underlined the importance of Japan's political and economic relations to Canada. I think it is true now that Japan is our third largest customer and is of vital importance in our developing markets for Canadian wheat in Asia. It is, of course, important that nothing should be done in

Proposed Legislation
either country to interfere with the healthy and important development of this trade between our two countries.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN
speechtext: As I said earlier, we in this group are very pleased that the premier of Japan was able to visit Canada. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the statement just made by our Prime Minister. I do not think there were any surprises in that statement. It was couched in the very careful diplomatic language that usually follows such a friendly visit from the head of a friendly government, but we hope that in the days ahead concrete advantages from this visit will flow to our country and to the people of Japan. We trust that everything possible will be done to increase trade and good economic relations between our countries.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN
speechtext: I do not want to indulge in debate, but with the permission of the house I should like to join with the Leader of the Opposition in his reference to Hon. T. C. Davis, whose contribution to those relations in question has been so outstanding and who through many years contributed so much not only to the province of Saskatchewan but also to the country as a whole.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN
speechtext: If I may crave the indulgence of the house I should like to associate myself in this regard with the words of the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister. Since I come from Saskatchewan I, of course, am well acquainted with the distinguished career of Hon. T. C. Davis in my province and the very valuable work he did on behalf of Canada for so many years. It was with great regret that we learned of his passing.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour; I am sorry I have not been able to send notice. My question arises out of countless protests that new regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act now defraud unemployed persons of holiday and severance pay by exercising a penalty before insurance benefits are paid. Is any consideration being given to rescinding these unfair regulations?

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, no consideration is being given at the moment to rescinding these regulations. As to the remark of the hon. member about defrauding, most certainly there is no intention on the part of the unemployment insurance commission to carry out any fraud with respect to those receiving benefits.

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: Was the advice of the unemployment insurance advisory committee sought before these unfair and vicious regulations were introduced?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: Order. The hon. member knows it is not proper in asking questions to make such positive statements of opinion. He is supposed to be seeking information. If he makes a statement of that kind he only invites debate, because obviously such expressions of opinion are not going to be accepted without challenge.

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: I wonder whether I might ask a further supplementary question. Was the advice of the unemployment insurance advisory committee sought before these sweeping new regulations were put into effect?

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: Has the minister or the department received protests from spokesmen for the trade union movement regarding these regulations?

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: May I, with the consent of the house, in view of the question which was put to me by the hon. member for Assiniboia- and I know this raises a matter which needs clarification in the minds of many hon. members of this house-as well as the charges which the hon. member made with respect to the regulation as it applies to vacation pay-be permitted to make a brief statement on the effects of this regulation at this time?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: Has the minister the leave of the house to make a more extensive answer regarding these regulations?

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext:
These regulations became effective on September 27 last, prior to which date there prevailed a situation whereby a claimant received unemployment insurance benefit and holiday pay at the same time. The purpose of unemployment insurance is to partially replace lost income and until that loss occurs benefit does not come into play.
Perhaps an explanation of the situation as it was prior to September 27 will help hon. members to understand why a change in the regulations was necessary. This was a common occurrence, and here is an example: a person separated from employment, say in November, was unable to obtain suitable employment and properly made a claim for, and was paid, unemployment insurance benefit. At that time any holiday pay he
Inquiries of the Ministry received was ignored. Subsequently this person obtained employment, but when a plant shut-down for holidays occurred at his new place of employment he had no holiday credits because of his short service. He again applied for, and was paid, unemployment insurance benefit. I feel sure we will all agree that one or at least part of one of these periods during which the man was not working must be recognized as a period of holiday. It is that recognition that the new regulation affords.
I might point out also that in the vast majority of these cases of benefit, it is not paid because of holiday pay. This is not lost entirely to the person, because the payment for the holiday is simply deferred to the end of the period.

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is it not true that the condition which now prevails under the new regulations applied prior to 1952 and was reversed at that time?

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. This was to rectify what was considered by the unemployment insurance commission as an anomaly and, in most cases, unfair treatment of the claimant.

subtopic: NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY

subtopic: DISARMAMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISARMAMENT
speechtext: I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if his attention has been directed to the statement in today's press attributed to the foreign minister of the so-called Chinese people's republic regarding current discussions on disarmament, and also the statement attributed to the state department of the United States commenting upon the views put forward by that foreign minister with respect to participation in disarmament discussions and the attitude that the government of China would take toward any disarmament treaty. Has the minister any comment which he feels might usefully be made at this time in view of the fact that Canada is a member of the ten power disarmament commission?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have seen two dispatches, one in the Gazette and the other in the Globe and Mail. The heading of the article in the Gazette is, I think, quite misleading. It says "Red China Demands Disarmament Role." Then the first paragraph reads:
Red China today served notice on the world it wants equal say with other big powers in any talks on global disarmament.
Then the next paragraph says this:
This was how many observers here interpreted a statement by Foreign Minister Chen Yi to a session of the standing committee of the national people's congress, China's parliament.
I think that certainly is not the interpretation to be put on the quoted words of the Chinese foreign minister, which appear farther down in the article:
China is ready unhesitatingly to commit itself to international obligations to which it agrees.
However, any international disarmament agreement which is arrived at without formal participation of the Chinese people's republic or the signature of its delegates cannot of course have any binding force on China.
Well, the hon. member will realize that every nation in the world is in that position; it would not be formally bound by any disarmament arrangement until it had agreed to that arrangement.
There is also a report in the Globe and Mail from Washington with a comment from the United States state department but it does not say that China is being asked to participate in the disarmament talks. The statement merely is that at some later stage perhaps there would be consultation. The actual situation is that at the Geneva

meetings last summer the United States, the United Kingdom, France and the Soviet union themselves set up this disarmament committee composed of five nations from the west and five nations from the east. Of course Canada is one of the five western nations, and there is no suggestion at all that there should be a change in that ten member disarmament committee.
We have pressed from the start for negotiations to be undertaken promptly because we feel it would be very disadvantageous to have any delay or stalling. As the hon. member knows, during the meetings in Paris in December the foreign ministers of the five western members of this disarmament committee met and invited the five eastern members to commence negotiations on March 15. This invitation was accepted and negotiations will commence on March 15. In addition, the five western nations met on January 18 in Washington to commence their preparations for the main meeting, and there is to be another meeting on January 25 in Washington. There is no suggestion that there should be a change in the plan to have these ten nations deal with negotiations on the question of disarmament.

subtopic: DISARMAMENT
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Would it be the view of the government that in the event of agreement on disarmament, the government of the Chinese people's republic would be asked to adhere or become obligated to its provisions in order to make disarmament generally effective?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
speechtext: No doubt that would be one of the questions which would be considered in due course. I believe we must take one step at a time in this new approach to disarmament. The immediate problem is to reach some agreement with the five eastern powers which are to be members of the ten power team.

subtopic: DISARMAMENT
speechtext:
May I
ask a supplementary question. Will the minister secure all the facts behind this news dispatch and later make a statement to the house as to the government's position with respect to this new development?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
speechtext:
I think I have already dealt with the question and made the government's position quite clear. I cannot go any farther, certainly at the present time. If there should be new developments, we will be very glad to take the house into our confidence.

subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA
speechtext: Arising out of the minister's reply, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he would comment on a report from Rangoon by the far eastern correspondent of the Toronto Globe and Mail that Canada has informed the Burmese government that Burma can expect nothing now under the Colombo plan except surplus food supplies, and that technical aid has been stopped?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA
speechtext:
Yes. I saw this dispatch, which had as the heading "Canada Yawns". I think the reporter who wrote that dispatch should yawn and wake up. The fact is that our relations with Burma are exceedingly good. I have here a statement which I was prepared to make yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, I have seen the news report to which my hon. friend has referred -

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA
speechtext: Order. In order to keep the record clear, I wonder whether the house would give the minister leave to make a statement at this time?

subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA
speechtext: I really am not making a statement, Mr. Speaker. I am answering a question and I welcome this opportunity to comment on it. The Leader of the Opposition was just a day late.

subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA
speechtext: You were a day late.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-REPORTED NON-APPLICATION TO BURMA
speechtext:
In the first place, the article says that Canada's role in providing aid to Burma has been limited to technical aid programs and the allocation of surplus food. The fact is that since 1957, in addition to substantial quantities of Canadian foodstuffs, Canada has agreed to provide capital and technical equipment worth over $578,000. This has included equipment for agricultural workshops, fisheries and prospecting equipment, a Canadian survey of highways in Burma, the provision of Canadian experts to Burma and the training of Burmese in this country, that is to say in Canada.
In addition, I can assure the house that the current aid program for Burma includes capital and technical assistance in addition to foodstuffs. As with all other Colombo plan countries, the Canadian aid program for Burma is worked out in detailed consultations with the Burmese government which are based on requests submitted by them. The program for Burma for 1959-60 is still

Inquiries of the Ministry being negotiated between Canadian and Burmese officials, and when these negotiations have been completed I will be pleased to inform the house of the details.
With regard to the statement in the article in the Globe and Mail that the Burmese government had been informed that henceforth they might expect to receive nothing but surplus foodstuffs from Canada, in view of what I have just said it will be clear that Canada has never made any such statement to the Burmese government. As a matter of fact, in November the Solicitor General visited Burma during the time he was in the Far East in connection with the Colombo plan meetings. He inspected some of the results of our aid to Burma, including a Cobalt bomb installation, and had a most friendly talk with members of the Burmese government. I had the same experience at the United Nations, where I struck up a firm friendship with the foreign minister of Burma; and our relations with that country, as I said in opening, are particularly good. I regret that a statement should have been published in the Canadian press of the nature of the one to which the Leader of the Opposition has referred.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Would he give information to the house as to any progress that has been made with respect to an offer I believe he made for the disposal of surplus pork so that it might get into the hands of charitable organizations and Indian and Eskimo residential schools, and perhaps into the hands of individuals who are in receipt of public welfare?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. Considerable interest has been shown in this offer. I wrote letters to the premiers of all the provinces making it known to them and asking them, if they were interested, to name somebody to deal with the stabilization board in securing supplies of this canned pork. We have now had replies from Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, all of whom have expressed interest in securing supplies. We have also had inquiries from a considerable number of charitable organizations. We have made arrangements to make certain amounts of pork available to some of those organizations-

The majority of them actually will secure their supplies through the pork we make available to the provincial governments.
We have also had a great deal of interest shown in this offer by international organizations. We have now had requests from CARE, the save the children fund, the Unitarian service committee of Canada, UNICEF, the Red Cross, Lutheran world relief, and the Canadian Council of Churches. Their requests up to date are for about 74 million pounds, and they have indicated that they would like to have considerably more than that. speechtext:
I shall be

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, January 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Emilien Morissette for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Argue.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke in the house on January 20, before this debate was interrupted, I was dealing generally with the question of immigration and had pointed to some of the things that I felt the facts establish about the contribution of the immigrant to the country's economy. I had made reference to some of the speeches that had been given on the subject by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) in the last few months. I had in mind particularly one that she made in the city of Vancouver on September 18 last, and in that part of her address in which she spoke in general terms about the advantages that derive from immigrants and from immigration the minister said this:
When they arrive they broaden the home market and provide new leeway and stimulus for economic development, make possible the improved location of industry, and the more efficient use of resources

spread the burden of overhead costs of government and utilities, and by strengthening the Canadian market reduce our reliance on imports and on export markets. In certain instances they relieve labour shortages, filling vacancies and thus facilitating fuller employment to many groups. In other instances they create entirely new industries and markets and make a major contribution to Canadian productivity. We must continue to attract them in the numbers we need for the orderly development of our country.
Anglo-Saxons are often heard to boast that we come from countries in which some of the most sacred principles of our law were cradled and in which were founded and established some of the ancient safeguards and procedures that we call in aid today in our courts. It is therefore of interest to study the immigrant for the purpose of determining the extent to which he has accommodated himself to the judicial system under which we live. As a lawyer who often had occasion, and often has occasion still, to practise in the criminal courts, I was quick to observe how rarely newcomers appeared before the criminal courts charged with serious breaches of the Criminal Code.
Realizing how, in so many cases, they had been required to so abruptly tear up the roots established in their homelands and had been deprived of so many opportunities-particularly the recent immigrants-in the formative years of their lives which were so sadly disrupted by war and the invasion of their countries; exposed as they were to a new country whose customs, habits and laws were often so different, I think it is some indication of the high calibre of our immigrant population to note how rarely we find them in difficulties with the law. In the year 1952, which is the last year for which I found the available figures, a total of 29,761 persons were found guilty of indictable offences in Canada. This would include the males admitted to penitentiaries and reformatories and would include all other persons convicted as well, regardless of whether they were sentenced to prison or were released on probation. Of that total of almost 30,000, 89.8 per cent were native born Canadians, and only 3 per cent of these crimes were found to have been committed by persons whose countries of origin were located in continental Europe. Indeed, this figure included many who had resided in our country for a long period of time.
These figures, it seems to me, and others I could give if I had the time, all tend to show that our immigrant population has a deep respect for our system of law and for the rules that have been promulgated for the common good of the people of Canada.
Once a policy is decided upon in such a field as immigration, such as the slow-down
The Address-Mr. Maloney policy which was designed to alleviate a growing unemployment problem, it follows that it must be enforced justly. This puts the minister in charge of the department in a very difficult position when exceptional cases arise for consideration. If exceptions are made they are used as precedents in future applications and, in the net result, chaos arises and you end up with almost no policy at all. However, our present policy in respect to immigration, necessitated as it has been by the belief of so many in the inexorable forces of economic circumstances, came for example at a bad time for the Polish people and for many thousands of Ukrainian people who now live within the boundaries of what is regarded as Poland.
In the last two years there has been a perceptible relaxation on the part of the Polish government in the numbers of its citizens and residents to whom it has permitted exit visas. Unfortunately this relaxation coincided with the corresponding restriction in our own country. Many worth-while persons residing in Poland today have a very deep longing to come to Canada and make it their home. They would make excellent citizens, and they have friends and relatives here who are well able to maintain them and ensure that that they would not become a charge on the state. I should like to see early steps taken, if this is feasible, to facilitate the entry into Canada of people who fall into that category.
There are also in Canada today large numbers who entered under the authority of a visitor's visa. Notwithstanding any undertaking they may have given not to apply for permanent landing, there are many of them who none the less are desirous of being given the status of landed immigrants. As I understand it, under present regulations, if they are justly enforced, this must be denied them and they are required to return to their countries of origin and there make application for the status they would like now to be given. Ordinarily many of the checks made in the case of an application for permanent landing are admittedly not made in the case of someone who applies for the status of a non-immigrant, but what I have in mind is some policy comparable to the one the government followed, I think it was in August, 1958, in the case of persons who were here on visitors' visas and to whom the government extended the privilege of permanent landing after an application had been made and a review of that application had been conducted.
From personal observation I would say there are many persons who fall into this category. I cannot help but feel they would make very desirable Canadian citizens. I should like to see some consideration given

The Address-Mr. Maloney to a plan, as I say, that would enable persons who fall into this category to remain here. I share the feeling of concern that is entertained by large numbers of fellow Canadians about our thinly populated country and its large geographical area, so much of it filled with great potential as yet untapped. I feel that the present sparsity of our population could, in the foreseeable future, pose one of our country's very serious problems. I do not think an immediately high birth rate, which of course would be very desirable, would provide anything like the numbers that I feel are required to help Canada accomplish what I conceive to be its full measure of development. I believe we need more people with capital, with energy, with skills; people with the ambitions of our forefathers when they came to make new homes, not alone for themselves but for their children and their children's children.
I picture this country as one that will grow increasingly in prestige and in stature among the nations of the world, populated by millions of freedom loving inhabitants with backgrounds and civilizations that are centuries old. Among other areas of our country capable, it would seem, of supporting a greatly increased population would be our great northwest. What the bolsheviks were able to do in the Arctic with slaves Canada, I think, would be able to do with ambitious pioneers and free men.
For the reasons I have given I should like to see the government take a new look at this whole question of immigration. The facts and figures to which I have referred, which are incontrovertible, tell me a true story; and if that be so, a vigorous policy on immigration started soon cannot, in my opinion, fail. It is bound, in whatever view you take of the matter, to succeed.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

The speech from the throne devoted a full paragraph to the subject of northern development and another full paragraph to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, but not a single word to the subject of the Atlantic provinces except for the mention of the repeal of the new fisheries board act relating to Newfoundland, which will be proposed during the present session. I am not against the development of the northern lands of Canada, but I repeat what I have said before in this house, namely, that before spending large sums of money for northern development consideration should be given to the development of existing resources in areas of Canada already inhabited, and I have particularly in mind the Atlantic provinces. Where is this decentralization of industry promised by the Conservative candidates in the Atlantic provinces before the last election? Where are the new crown corporations promised to be established in the

Atlantic provinces? What about the construction of the Chignecto canal? What progress has been made toward the realization of this particular project of major importance to the people of New Brunswick? What progress has the government made on the construction of the causeway to link Prince Edward Island with New Brunswick? We heard the statement made this morning by the Minister of Public Works which shows that very little progress has been made in this field.
I know that before the Prince Edward Island provincial election last summer this project was by all means the major promise made to the electors of the island. In fact the present government of Prince Edward Island was called the causeway government. But only a few weeks after the election the present Minister of Public Works found out there were many objections in the way, and that it would be rather difficult to proceed with the construction of this causeway on account of tremendous problems. It is amazing to realize that such objections could come into existence only after the provincial election, and still more amazing it is to note the reaction of the present premier of Prince Edward Island who, when asked to comment on the statement by the Minister of Public Works, said, "I am satisfied with the statement". How easy they are to satisfy now that they are in power.
The Atlantic provinces are confronted with most serious basic economic problems which cannot be resolved by ad hoc provisions which we can qualify as first aid measures of political expediency. Such patch-up measures have not brought and will never bring the economy of the Atlantic region in line with other sections of the country.
The time has come for the federal government to initiate measures of such magnitude and such scope as to effectively assist the economy of the Atlantic region, even if it has to be something exceptional, something of a scope this nation has not attempted before. If special tax concessions must be granted by Ottawa to industries established in the Atlantic region, this matter should receive full study and consideration. As transportation difficulties seem to be one of the major handicaps to Atlantic development, this matter should also receive full consideration.
One of the most urgent needs of the Atlantic provinces is a substantial Atlantic provinces special investment fund for the purpose of financing large projects so essential to further economic development of the primary industries in these provinces. In the last decade or so federal projects of major importance have been undertaken in other sections of central Canada, outside of the Atlantic region. I have in mind particularly the St. Lawrence 79951-0-15
The Address-Mr. Pigeon seaway, which has just been completed; the south Saskatchewan dam project, which is now under way; and I could add the hundreds of millions of dollars which are being spent by the federal government right here in the capital city of Ottawa. No need for me to emphasize also the part played by the federal treasury for the prairie provinces, and I could also mention the proposed Columbia river development in British Columbia, which is receiving the attention of the government at the present time.
I repeat that one of the major handicaps in the development of our Atlantic provinces is the transportation problem. It is true that the federal government has been contributing for a number of years to the construction of the trans-Canada highway, but in this case our Atlantic provinces shared in the cost in the same proportion as other provinces of Canada, with the exception of the province of Quebec. The fact that our Atlantic provinces participated in this trans-Canada highway program has placed a heavy debt burden on their population. In fact when we consider that the average mileage of trans-Canada highway in New Brunswick is .76 per 1000 of population as compared with .32 in Ontario, it gives an idea of the share we have to pay for the construction of the trans-Canada highway.
The taxes, both municipal and provincial, imposed on our population are out of line with other sections of the country. In order to relieve our provincial treasurers and benefit the taxpayers accordingly I would suggest that every consideration be given by the federal government to compensating the Atlantic provinces by special assistance or concessions for the construction and maintenance of our highways. This, Mr. Speaker, is not asking too much, and it could be one way for the majority of the Canadian people to give moral and financial support to the economy of the Atlantic region.
This could be a far reaching program, but anyone willing to listen to the plight of the Atlantic provinces will fully realize that more than the ordinary type of federal assistance, something exceptional, should be put forward to restore in the Atlantic provinces an economic climate which will compare favourably with that of the rest of Canada.

I thought it would be advisable, Mr. Speaker, to choose the textile industry as the subject matter of my remarks, a choice which seems to me highly consistent as the textile industry has indeed a prominent place and therefore plays a vital part in the economy of my district and of my province. I intend to deal with the sad plight of that industry with all the vigour called for in view of its distressing condition. The representatives of the western provinces are rightly known for their persistence when asking for legislation which they deem essential to the advance and welfare of those provinces. A representative of the ancient province of Quebec has, therefore, no reason to feel embarrassed when in his turn he asks for the urgent and necessary remedies which would bring about a fair solution of the complex issues which our textile industry has been facing for many years in all the eastern provinces and more particularly in Quebec. I trust I shall find among the members from the west, when discussing the difficulties in which the textile industry finds itself, the same understanding and comprehension as I give them when they deal with the matter of wheat.
In Quebec nobody is indifferent to the plight of the textile industry, and rightly so. This ancient industry has for a long time been identified with the economy of the province of Quebec. It is a well known fact that capital investments in the Canadian and Quebec textile industries are for the greater part made by Canadian citizens. As a matter of


fact, their capital is owned by Canadians to the extent of 80 per cent in comparison with a proportion of 52 per cent in the other manufacturing and mining industries. This statement may be found in the Gordon report. The textile industry appears, therefore, particularly Canadian and deserves as such, if not favoured treatment, at least the highest measure of equitable consideration. (Translation):
In the last few years and in spite of more or less brilliant prospects, our textile industry did not hesitate confidently to invest new funds in the modernization of its equipment, in the renewal of its machinery and in the restoration of its spinning mills. In the period extending from 1947 to 1958, capital investments in the textile industry reached a total of $305.7 millions. Therefore in our progressive era, that industry cannot be accused of being satisfied with out-dated facilities and obsolete production methods.
It should also be stressed that industrial relations in the textile industry are characterized by a close and fruitful co-operation between management and labour, for they realize that the stability of a company and the security of its staff are interdependent. In that regard an important textile labour union has been twice known to express before the tariff board claims with regard to tariff that were entirely identical to those of the management in the same industry. This means that, in the textile industry, labour and management think that their interests are interdependent rather than opposed and that they behave more as partners than as opponents. In the textile industry, we find a team spirit which might serve as an example to industries throughout this country.
Am I right, Mr. Speaker, when I say that the textile industry is among the first in my province? I hope I shall convince you without difficulty as my contention is easy to illustrate.
The textile industry ranks high in the province of Quebec with regard to level of employment: more than 38,000 workers earn a livelihood. In Joliette, which is the principal industrial centre of the constituency I represent in this house, approximately 700 workers earn their livelihood from the textile industry.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I have the honour of counting among my constituents the premier of the province of Quebec.

Therefore, I may say that in the province of Quebec in general and more particularly in Joliette, the textile industry is an outstanding source of employment. As a result, thousands of families in Quebec depend on the textile industry for their livelihood. That is why any slowdown in that industry results in complete unemployment for thousands of workers; or, which is not much better, reduces the working week to three or four days, which means partial unemployment.
My city of Joliette and other textile centres in Quebec have suffered terribly from total or partial unemployment which was the inevitable result of the stoppage or the slowing down of production in the last few years throughout that industry. But that is not all, Mr. Speaker, the level of employment is undoubtedly an important factor in the textile industry; there is, however, another factor which may be still more significant. I refer to the decentralization which is characteristic of the Canadian textile industry. The spinning mills are distributed all over the province; they are widely spread in various Quebec centres. Not a single other industry is disseminated to such an extent and in so many communities, large, medium or small, in the province. The Gordon report shows that the 745 textile companies of that area are distributed in 218 different communities, emphasizing that the textile industry is a "small town" industry.
One readily realizes the immense social advantage which can be derived from such decentralization of the textile industry.
That industry, as everyone knows, employs mostly young female workers. The young people living in small textile centres can get jobs on the spot, and do not have to go to larger centres to earn their living, with the result that family cohesion is greatly strengthened. Extra farm hands in rural areas, where the small textile centres are located, also find on the spot a steady source of employment. This avoids the social uprooting involved by the shifting of rural labour towards larger urban centres.
A third factor, more important perhaps than the first two I have mentioned, which explains why the textile industry is so closely integrated to the local community, is that numerous textile centres are all that the name implies, in that they often constitute the sole industry in the community.
Allow me to mention as an example, Mr. Speaker, the case of Magog, in the province of Quebec, where 83.4 per cent of the labour 79951-0-15i
The Address-Mr. Pigeon force derive their livelihood from the local textile industry. At St. Gregoire de Montmorency, which has a population of 6,077, 1,651 persons earn their living in the local textile industry. In such cases, the whole economy of the textile community depends exclusively on the textile industry. Any production stoppage or slowing down, in such cases, means total or partial unemployment for the whole active population. And when the textile industry of such communities is in the grips of a permanent production stoppage, the result is an extremely tragic social drama, since whole families, who have always earned their living in the local textile industry, must leave their homes where they have lived for years, give up the only trade they know and expatriate themselves in order to earn a livelihood, in spite of untold difficulties, in a new environment and in a different job.
One must also consider, Mr. Speaker, that, as a rule, the textile industry's most productive period is between November and May, that is during seasonal unemployment brought about by our climate; and that the textile industry, if it produced at full capacity in the winter months, could thus absorb a substantial proportion of workers faced with unemployment during that period of the year.
You will readily understand, Mr. Speaker, after those few remarks, that the textile industry undoubtedly has a unique role to play in the over-all industrial pattern of my city and province, both from the economic and social standpoint.
At first, you will be inclined to say that there is no reason why the production of the textile industry should not remain at the present level or should not increase, since that industry produces articles which are essential to a civilized society. That industry produces things which are necessary for the community. It does not produce items which are merely useful, and still less, superfluous. The textile industry is vital in our modern world. One cannot possibly imagine an organized community without a textile industry.
In fact, consumption of textile products is increasing constantly, due to the increase in population, and the higher standard of living.
Under such circumstances, how is it that the textile industry, far from constantly increasing its production, must frequently interrupt it, slow it down or stop it altogether? That brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the core of the problem which the textile industry has been facing for too long.

In the textile industry salaries are an important item of the production cost. Let me explain. Out of every dollar spent in the production of textile, nearly 60 per cent or roughly 60 cents is given in salary to the textile worker, which goes to prove that salaries are a substantial item in the textile industry.
Now, salaries paid to Canadian textile workers are from 100 to 800 per cent higher than those paid to foreign textile workers, except in the United States. What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that the Canadian textile industry is paying its labour twice as much as the British textile industry, three or four times more than the European textile industry and nine times more than the Asiatic textile industry. As an example, Japanese textile workers earn 14 cents an hour.
Salaries in the textile industry, averaging as I said, Mr. Speaker, 60 per cent of the production cost, one readily understands that if the Canadian textile industry pays salaries two to nine times higher than those paid by the British, European and Asiatic textile industries, the production cost of the Canadian textile industry is necessarily much higher than the cost of production of the foreign textile industry, with the result that, all things being equal, the Canadian textile industry is unable to compete with the foreign textile industry on the domestic market.
With regard to the United States, it is not the difference in salaries which creates a problem for the Canadian textile industry, although as a result of the removal of American textile plants from the northern to southern United States, it may happen that salaries paid by the Canadian textile industry are higher than those in some American textile plants located in the southern states.
The U.S. textile industry has a production capacity ten times higher than that of the Canadian textile industry; and this is, of course, because the United States have a population ten times larger than ours and because their textile industry has a market ten times greater than ours.
At the end of the operating season, if the U.S. textile industry is left with a production surplus of 2 per cent, which is a very small proportion of its mass production, and if it disposes of it on the Canadian market at a price slightly lower than the U.S. price, it


means that with such a production surplus of 2 per cent the U.S. textile industry secures 20 per cent of the Canadian market at the expense of our own textile industry, which cannot compete with the lower U.S. prices on the Canadian market. Now, in 1957, the United States exported about 218 million yards of cotton goods to Canada. And the volume of employment in the Canadian textile industry decreases as U.S. textile exports increase. We And proof of this, Mr. Speaker, in the fact that over a seven year period only, the number of persons employed in the textile industry has decreased from 46,000 in 1950, to 38,500 in 1957.
I am not asking that a China Wall be built around the Canadian market to protect our textile industry. I know too well that our country has to import if it wants to export. But I think that we should give back to our textile industry the share of the home market that it had a quarter of a century ago. At that time, our textile industry was supplying 75 per cent of the needs of the Canadian market, but today its share has been reduced to 50 per cent. Imports of cotton textiles have increased from 56 million yards in 1932 to 265 million yards in 1957; with the result, as I have just said, that the market for our textile products, in our own country, has substantially decreased because of an unbearable and untenable competition, since our textile industry now supplies only 50 per cent of our domestic needs, instead of 75 per cent, 25 years ago.
I am not suggesting that our textile industry be granted a monopolistic hold on the Canadian market; it is not asking for that either. But what can rightfully be claimed is that our textile industry be granted an equitably and reasonably larger share of the Canadian market. And this can be done without creating any international complications and without spoiling our good neighbour relations with the United States.
I know, sir, that we have to export our metals, our wheat and our oil. But allowing foreign or American textile products such an easy access to our home markets has not, as far as I know, brought about an equally easy access for our own products on foreign or American markets. I do not know that for each yard of textile fabric, foreign or American, imported in Canada, we have succeeded in exporting to the United States or to other countries one pound of metal, one gallon of oil or one bushel of wheat more.

Trade relations are not a one way street. The problems of the textile industry should not be allowed to last nor to worsen under the fallacious pretence that a more adequate tariff policy or more appropriate duties would be detrimental to other industries or to the agriculture of Canada.
It would be unfair if the trade policy of Canada did not take into account in its objectives, the present plight of the textile industry, or failed to realize the distressing condition of the textile industry is the price or the ransom that we have to pay for our other commercial transactions with the United States and the rest of the world.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that stronger protective measures, or rather a greater measure of justice, in favour of the textile industry on the part of the government would not create international complications and, I repeat, would not cause frictions with our American neighbours, whose textile production would be hardly affected while ours would be substantially increased.
I know, sir, that the problems of the textile industry are of little concern to our friends opposite.
In fact, I think I should mention this, Mr. Speaker: on March 9, 1954, the hon. Mr. McCann, then Minister of National Revenue, received a delegation of the union of the textile workers of America. He then said to representatives of the textile workers that the Canadian textile industry was overexpanded.

Our region derives a great deal of its development and prosperity from the products of its forests. We are a great centre of pulp and paper manufacturing, 95 per cent of which is being exported to the United States, and the same can be said about the rich iron ore of Steep Rock iron mines, which within five years will ship eight to nine million tons of ore annually valued at $100 million to our neighbour to the south.
This, of course, sounds good but the fact that our Canadian dollar sells at a premium of approximately 5 to 6 per cent over the United States dollar makes Canadian pulp and paper, especially, more expensive and we are faced with keen competition from other countries in this market which has always been looked upon as our own preserve. The crux of the question is that we cannot afford the luxury of maintaining the price of the dollar above that of the United States. To have the most valuable dollar in the world may be a source of great Canadian pride, but unfortunately if it is going to remain high it will have the effect of reducing income from sales which are made, and encourage Canadian purchases of products of other countries.
To bring the Canadian dollar to parity with the United States dollar is, I believe, one of the very first objectives of this government. Nearly three quarters of a billion dollars worth of iron ore is being sold annually to the United States and approximately a quarter of a million is sold to other countries.
If we were to consider trade alone, our dollar would be worth 95 cents and not $1.05 in terms of United States dollar value, because of our trade deficit. What keeps our dollar high as every one knows is the inflow of fresh investments and the borrowing of our provincial and municipal governments along with private corporations. According to official figures, United States capital in Canada represents about 52 per cent of total investment in manufacturing, mining, oil and gas. It can be and has been said that we are purchasing our prosperity by giving title to our resources to outsiders.
Why should not the government give active encouragement to the establishment of steel mills in Canada which would make use of our rich iron ore? A steel mill at the lake-head would be the logical location to serve the needs of western Canada and the far north, using the nearby iron ore from Steep Rock iron mines.
In the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur we are particularly fortunate in our

labour and management relationships. There have never been any serious, protracted strikes. This fortunate situation is mainly due to a reasonable attitude taken by labour and to a sympathetic and understanding management. But we have often felt the strain and consequences of strikes alsewhere in the nation.
I should like to suggest that the federal government while it is engaged in appointing royal commissions on almost every problem affecting our economy should seriously consider the establishment of a management-labour commission which would sit continuously, assessing problems of industry and conditions of labour. This body could also carry on a study of the question of our older workers. In this connection I should like to pay tribute to my good friend, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) who has been trying to encourage employers to eliminate restrictive hiring policies based on broad assumptions which brand workers over 40 as undesirable for employment.
News stories of people reaching and passing the century mark are commonplace. It is a well-established fact that the life span of Canadians has increased greatly and if this prolongation of life continues during the next 50 years, at the pace established during the past 50 years, we will be faced with a whole new set of circumstances and problems, social as well as economic. There is no one who denies that medical science has extended life expectancy to such an extent that the time has come when governments together with labour and industry should make a concerted reappraisal of methods dealing with the placement of older workers. One of the difficulties in placing older workers appears to be just an old prejudice rather than a doubt of an older person being able to perform a job effectively.
I am one of those who believes that a reassessment of our entire retirement policy is due for a revision. With the life span increasing, at the rate estimated by the medical profession, I would say that in the foreseeable future the age of retirement may well be 75 years of age rather than the now generally accepted standard of 65, and at the same time-people in poor health- should qualify for pension at 60 or even 55.

the right to bargain in a similar manner to members of police and fire departments.
To deny these fundamental rights to an important sector of our population is to stamp our federal government policies with the seal of antiquity in dealing with its employees. I expect that the policies of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will come up again for review during this session of parliament. However, there should be some standards set which would prevent certain programs offensive to good taste from being piped into Canadian homes. By and large the standard of programming is not bad, but occasionally some presentations are on the borderline of being horror pictures which should not be allowed.
On a previous occasion I expressed my disgust at an offensive T.V. program produced by the C.B.C. for which I was criticized by some press reporters, and they may exercise their privilege to criticize me again for what I am about to say about another C.B.C. television program which appeared on Sunday, January 3.
This particular program had originally been intended for the General Motors Presents series, sponsored by General Motors of Canada. Following a screening of the drama, General Motors withdrew its sponsorship. I extend my warmest congratulations to Mr. Larry Gough, head of the public relations department of that company for refusing to accept the play, which, while of literary value for an adult informed audience, was hardly a fit play for general consumption. Mr. Gough described the play as "grim". Even the C.B.C. script chief, Mr. Leslie McFarlane, said that the "Shadow of a Pale Horse" was a pretty grim thing. When the royal commission on freight rates was appointed the people at the lake-head were assured that the commission would hold a hearing at the lakehead to consider the iniquities which are stifling the progress of northwestern Ontario. A few weeks ago, we were informed that the royal commission would meet only in the capital cities of the provinces. Thus we are going to witness the spectacle of a hearing in the city of Toronto which the premier of the province had not even asked for until the lakehead had made the request for a hearing to solve the crucial freight rate problem that plagues northwestern Ontario. It is rather disappointing that the very first action of this commission after the appointment of Mr. MacPherson, Q.C., of Regina, as its chairman, was the rejection of the northwest request for a hearing. May I point out that as the people of Manitoba are penalized somewhat to the same extent as northwestern Ontario, the freight rate problem is of mutual concern to both this region and the prairie provinces.
This section of the province of Ontario has been for a long time in a very precarious competing position with respect to the other sections of the province and will remain in an inferior position so long as the railways continue their freight rates structure on a horizontal basis. Their inequalities were brought to the attention of the House of Commons committee during the last session of parliament. Just to give you an example of what I mean by inequalities, you can ship a carload of lumber from the west coast to Toronto at a cheaper rate than from the lakehead to Toronto.
Officials of Steep Rock iron mines have made the statement that investment capital will not come to northwestern Ontario to help develop iron ore reserves owing to high freight rates. They stated that it costs $2 per ton to ship iron ore from Port Arthur while it costs only $1.63 to ship ore the same distance from Seven Islands to Philadelphia.
When the 17 per cent increase was allowed in November, 1958, and was reduced to 10 per cent effective on August 1, 1959, eight of the provinces protested the 17 per cent increase; Ontario and Quebec remained silent as the sphinx. Now we see Premier Frost climbing on the band wagon for a hearing in Toronto. Toronto is not interested in freight rates, and if they are genuinely interested in helping northwestern Ontario then the premier should have asked that the hearing be held at the lakehead instead of Toronto.
Nothing that has happened in the past, and nothing that can really happen in the near future, will have such a telling effect on the development of northwestern Ontario as freight rates. This is a problem which transcends political party lines and takes precedence over all regional matters because it affects the future of this great area of 200,000 square miles right up to the border of Manitoba.
I submit that the royal commission must see this grain port terminal, this new midcontinental seaport, this fabulous store of natural resources, and hear from the people concerned how equitable freight rates could bring about an era of prosperity for all of Canada.
In the belief that my constituents would expect me to say a word about the lake-head seaway terminal dock which now is actually under construction, with work on the fourth stage contract due to start in the near future, I express the hope that the new Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) will approve in the budget estimates the funds necessary to carry on the project without any delays.
And here, I wish to quote Mr. L. C. Irwin, chairman of the lakehead harbour commission, who also happens to be the district manager of the Searle Grain Elevators. Speaking of the first year of the seaway operation with regard to the lakehead he said this:
Locally, 1959 is bound to go down in history as the year the Lakehead Harbour Commission was formed, and it is extremely important to note that to hold our place on the shipping scenes of the world, we must realize the dire necessity of sending more and more of our grain direct to overseas markets in ocean-going bottoms.
No fewer than 131 ships from overseas called at the ports of Fort William and Port Arthur and of these 75 picked up grain for overseas ports and five took flour; all of the latter headed for west African ports. Combined outgoing grain figures in deep sea bottoms, including overseas and inland, amounted to 31,736,000 bushels.
It can readily be seen that the lakehead harbour will become one of the important ports of the world. However, there is one definite obstacle in the way of keeping this seaport open as long as possible and that is the lack of tug and ice breaking facilities available. Last spring ocean ships were having difficulties at the lakehead harbours due to not having tug assistance. We used to have one a couple of years ago which was named the Whalen. This was transferred to some other port and we were promised that a replacement with the new tug and icebreaker Alexander Henry was to take over.

To this day we do not know the reason why this tug is stationed at some port on the Georgian bay. I submit to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) that the question of tug and icebreaking service is absolutely essential at the lakehead if we are to take every advantage of the new seaway, and this service should be reinstated on a year-round basis.
The Canadian Farm Loan Board Act was originally established for the purpose of helping farmers and would-be farmers to improve their holdings and to establish young men willing to take up farming. Unfortunately, this board did not concern itself too much with the smaller farmers of northwestern Ontario. Now we have the farm credit corporation, successors to the Canadian farm loan board. When the change of name was made it gave some hope that its policy would be more considerate to the needs of the farmers as found in the district of Thunder Bay, but unfortunately I have evidence that such is not the case.
A farmer by the name of Herbert Russell, of the village of Murillo, capable conscientious and as honest as the day is long, applied for a loan to improve his holdings and was turned down. Last October I wrote the board on behalf of the applicant, asking for a reconsideration, and the reply I received was a recommendation that Mr. Russell submit a new application to the new farm credit corporation. I have heard nothing since.
A Mr. Henry Erickson of the village of Nolalu, a farmer who has lived on his land for 35 years, applied for a modest loan of $2,000 on 300 acres. His farm is valued at approximately $5,000 and the loan was turned down.
I cannot fathom the thinking of this new crown corporation which appears to be in business to help the needy but which in reality only wishes to help those whose collateral gives the privilege of borrowing at any bank without the assistance of the corporation.
This government has failed to establish a definite policy of farm assistance for areas such as northwestern Ontario, and practically the same can be said about the lack of enthusiasm shown by the government in assisting small businesses by making loans available to them, notwithstanding repeated statements to the contrary by members of the government. The truth of the matter may be found in the tight money situation which in large measure is the result of the huge deficits of the federal government. The Liberal government of Louis St. Laurent paid its way and had a sizeable surplus available for tax reduction and debt retirement, thus making easy money available for small business and industrial expansion.
