Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to say how happy I am to see you and all the other members of the house apparently in good health and in good spirits. I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on his recent election to the high office of Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees. I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Morissette) and seconder (Mrs. Casselman) respectively for the way in which they carried out their duties with regard to the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
In recent times I have received a considerable amount of correspondence relative to the efficiency of government. Several weeks ago I learned from the press that the Canadian chamber of commerce had made certain representations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in this connection and therefore I was very happy when he announced to the house on January 18 that the government intends to establish a royal commission to recommend means of running the government more efficiently and that this commission would be set up along the lines of the United States Hoover commission which recommended methods and procedures for reducing government expenditures to the lowest amount consistent with the efficient functioning of government. I support such an investigation and I especially welcome the interest of various individuals and groups in this regard. They can contribute much in experience and knowledge to assist the royal commission by briefs and the like in obtaining that degree of efficiency which is of paramount importance in the operation of our government.
Every business as a rule has two kinds of financial statements. One of these is called income and disbursements and the other is called assets and liabilities. Both of these might well be used in governmental affairs and especially, I think, both of these should be applied in our evaluation of our natural


resources. I do not think that enough attention has been paid to the latter aspect, that is, our assets and liabilities in the field of our natural resources.
Such a statement of Canada's liabilities would, of course, show an obligation to feed and clothe a rapidly increasing population. On the other hand, our assets would raise a question whether they are sufficiently conserved and renewed to match this need.
We are told today that our timber and pulp resources and production of these resources are decreasing rather than increasing. It was, therefore, a matter of some satisfaction to me that the government announced in the speech from the throne that it would ask parliament to authorize the establishment of a new department to be concerned with affairs relating to the forests and their most effective utilization and conservation, and to assume responsibility for other related resources. I think this is a step that might well have been taken some years ago.
It is startling to learn that only about 3 per cent of Canada is suitable for agriculture and that we are steadily losing even this limited asset. Besides continuing losses due to soil erosion, we are losing some of our very best land in southern Ontario and elsewhere because of unplanned development. We see in expanding urban areas a great many acres of our best land being used for building purposes, land that will be lost forever to us as food producing areas. One wonders whether our development in this field is following a sound course. Perhaps we should be examining the situation as it is found in Europe and elsewhere where every piece of productive land is jealously guarded by society and building takes the form of high-rise apartments rather than individual dwellings occupying considerable acreage of fertile soil.
In some parts of our country we are losing acres and acres of land because it is unsuitable for modern tractor operation and has now resulted in uneconomical farming. These economic and sociological problems pertaining to our agricultural resources should receive as much close attention as our forestry assets and other resources, renewable and otherwise.
The first and possibly the most important step to be taken in solving these problems is a stocktaking of the amount and quality of our present resources, including amongst other things our productive soil assets. This could be reduced to a per capita basis, so we could fully appreciate the real significance of our reducing assets and increasing liabilities in this regard.

Such a statement of our assets would serve governmental policy, while our statement of income and expenditures would serve the cause of efficiency. For example, every businessman reduces his cost of production to a unit basis in an attempt to improve his position. Why should the government not do likewise? Again, every businessman makes certain that the benefits of his operation are greater than his costs because otherwise he would lose money. Our government, then, seeking to develop our national resources and to increase national wealth should make even greater use of cost-benefit studies before expending large sums of tax money on new projects.
I believe the time has come for us to develop a regional survey library which would help us greatly in obtaining a national resources inventory. There is much information available already in various fields obtained by various agencies and various levels of government which should be centralized in such a library so that the cost of future planning would be reduced to a minimum by the elimination of the duplication of work which has already been done. In saying this, I should like also to underline the fact that it is most important that appropriate checks be made on any project which is being contemplated, especially through a cost-benefit study before the project is finally undertaken.
I was very pleased with the action taken by the government to amend the Railway Act to permit certain grants to be made from the railway grade crossing fund for a further period of three years beyond January 31, 1961. I have always considered the problem arising from the dangers inherent in railway-highway crossings to be one which requires the fullest co-operation and consideration of the federal government and of all other responsible parties. It is true that our country is large and that we have many such crossings. However, it seems to me that a vast program for the elimination of level crossings, especially on our trans-Canada highways and other heavily travelled thoroughfares in densely populated areas, might be considered as a practical and fitting way to mark our national progress. The completion of such an undertaking in time for our centennial in 1967 would be especially desirable. This scheme would create a sound public works program which would make many new jobs available across the entire country and in all the heavily urbanized areas.
I was pleased to hear in the speech from the throne that measures will be proposed to amend the Old Age Security Act and the Veterans Allowance Act to establish a basis
The Address-Mr. Kucherepa for the payment of pensions and allowances to Canadians residing outside of Canada. There are now many worthy cases which require this amount of consideration from the standpoint of health and for other personal reasons. In this regard, we would be following the usage which has been adopted in the United Kingdom and in other countries.
I should like to say something on this occasion by way of suggesting to the government that they investigate the possibility of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 183, which was passed by parliament in 1938 and which provides for loans to municipalities by the federal government to enable a municipality to undertake certain self-liquidating public works projects. One of the conditions of this act is that its application assists in the relief of unemployment in a given municipality. Under this act, which now requires some up to date revision, low interest rate loans could be made available to hard-pressed municipalities. This could provide a means of attacking the problem of seasonal unemployment. I suggest this plan for the consideration of the government.
Over one quarter of the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, was devoted to matters dealing with international affairs. This is significant of the degree of importance international affairs play in our daily lives. Today, January 22, is a memorable day for many of our fellow Canadians of Ukrainian descent. Forty two years ago in the capital city of the Ukraine, the Ukrainian people proclaimed their independence from Moscow domination. One year later on the same date, January 22, 1919, the western territories of the Ukraine which had been submerged in the Austro-Hungarian empire for many decades were reunited with the Ukraine into one sovereign state under one independent government. This independent Ukrainian republic was the first nation to accept the offer of coexistence with the Russians, and likewise it was the first nation to be subjugated soon thereafter. I know that members of the house will join with me in expressing to the Ukrainian people and to our fellow Canadians of Ukrainian descent our sincere hope that the Ukrainian nation, along with other enslaved nations, will one day again enjoy liberty and freedom in the society of free nations.
In the light of history, it seems that Mr. Khrushchev's coexistence offer means primarily getting along with Soviet Russia as much as possible on Moscow's terms and at her pleasure. This is the main proposal made by Mr. Khrushchev both before and after his recent trip to the United States of

The Address-Mr. Kucherepa America. It is most important that everyone concerned in international affairs be cognizant of this fact. The leaders of the Kremlin might consider this to be a good and tried method of psychological warfare on their part. On the other hand, the leaders of the free world, and in the uncommitted countries, could be eventually oriented to the true facts of the international situation and so evolve a policy on international matters which I shall describe as positive.
Such a policy will not only maintain world peace but will also promote the cause of freedom and the complementary regression of communist growth. What do I mean when I speak of a positive policy? A positive policy is first of all a realistic policy, devoid of wishful thinking, sometimes also called selfdeception; a policy which is dedicated to preserving the highest principles and spiritual values of our free way of life. The failure to develop such an international policy could be, in the long run, disastrous to our freedom.
What are the prerequisites of such a policy? I should like to touch briefly on some. First of all, we must give some thought to our spiritual values. Communism, limited as it is to economic and materialistic objectives, could never defeat such a superior ideology which is our heritage. This should be the keystone of our policy in international affairs even as it should be, and I know it is, in our national affairs. I am sure that such a concept would be acceptable to the great majority of mankind.
Second, we must maintain our military defence at full strength. Disarmament talks mean little if effective proposals for real control are not forthcoming. It is the sincere hope, I know, of every one of us that through patient negotiation we can attain in the near future that degree of disarmament which will make aggression impossible.
We must avoid wishful thinking when we deal with the leaders of the Kremlin. We must come to understand fully their attitudes and mentality, remembering their fundamental indoctrination that an agreement is to be respected only if it is useful to the communist cause. Their record in this connection is only too well known and presents one of the greatest obstacles in resolving the problems which beset the world today. Any agreement made with the Kremlin must be subject to some kind of joint international control. This is the only feasible course to follow until such time as the communist leaders shall have proven by deeds that they will live up to their international commitments and promises.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say something about summit meetings. We should

be fully aware of all the implications of summit meetings. On the one hand, because there appears to be no other effective means of negotiating with Soviet leaders, they might bring about earlier decisions on a given number of questions; on the other hand, we must remember that, if gravely unsuccessful, they could precipitate dangerous situations. Need I mention Munich?
However, if we have a policy based on what I have just said in the last few minutes, and being fully mindful of the communist position, our leaders acting calmly and wisely might eke out certain benefits from such meetings. One of these might well be a fuller understanding and a deeper comprehension of the communist make-up and a fuller appreciation of the degree of sincerity of the communist leaders as well as a better assessment of the possibility of achieving tangible results from further discussions and negotiations. This kind of knowledge could be of great importance in determining certain policy decisions on our part. No politician or businessman, being fully informed, would adopt a course or policy which, although appearing beneficial at the moment, had the earmarks of certain disaster in the near future.
As long as there is no agency capable of acting as mediator or judge above nations however large or small they may be, there can be no absolute ground rules laid down for dealing with international problems. Therefore, it is necessary to conduct ourselves according to the rules as they are formulated and as they exist, and not according to the rules as we should like them to be. I hope that we shall never practise self-deception in this matter.
Every move which the communist camp makes should be matched by a counter-move on our part. We have been strictly on the defensive for too long; the time to draw a line in this regard is long past due. We should be waging our own ideological offensive. Instead, we continually find ourselves on the defensive.
What about the captive nations of eastern Europe? Without a positive solution to their problems there is scant hope that any degree of European security can be achieved, and without that how can we anticipate lasting world peace? We must be frank with ourselves. The basic decisions taken at Yalta after the second world war have not worked out satisfactorily. Let us therefore not be hesitant in utilizing our best efforts in putting these matters straight. We have our responsibilities in this matter. What we need now is the courage to put our case, which is a just one, on the agenda.

Our most difficult years are behind us. I believe we have stemmed the ideological invasion by communism. The time has now come for us to move ahead and to take the ideological initiative in pressing the case for human dignity and liberty which is still the most powerful force motivating mankind. This is now being dramatically demonstrated on the African continent as we see race after race achieve nationhood. We must continue to strive for this goal, as this is the only way in which we can hope to achieve lasting world peace with justice.
There has been much talk about increasing trade with the communists. I believe this talk originated as the result of a trial balloon put forth by Mr. Khrushchev. This is the battleground which the communists have chosen; this is the means which they are using to avoid an ideological struggle which they fear. With their slave labour and exploitation of the masses they would have a tremendous edge in this kind of a struggle. There are a great number of business leaders both here in Canada and in the United States of America who have been enthralled by this bait. Whether these people are thinking of a fast profit or whether they are just naive or whether they sincerely believe in the possibilities contained in these trial balloons, I would rather not say. However, I will say that the integration to any considerable degree of the economy of any free country to that of the communist bloc would in a short time spell disaster for that country.
Speaking in London, England, in the Albert Hall on November 4, 1958, our Prime Minister said this:
The communist world having changed its direction from open to concealed aggression to trade requires counteraction by the free world.
He then went on to say this:
Trade has become a major weapon in the communist world offensive. First it was the U.S.S.R. and now red China has joined in an Asian onslaught, intended to capture markets and with and through them, the minds of men. The communist drive is designed to undermine the economic strength of the free world.
It is obvious then that by tying free nations of the world to the communist economic machine on the one hand, while forcing them out of their present markets on the other hand, the Kremlin is seeking to gain complete economic control of these countries, after which they feel political conquest would be a simple proposition.
Our energies today should be directed mainly in two fields in so far as trade is concerned. First, we should do all we can to assist the underdeveloped countries to get on their feet. Once their economies are put into high gear with all its resultant demands we can anticipate an increasing volume of
The Address-Mr. Regier trade with these people. This would be a policy of enlightened self-interest. We are in this country to a considerable degree now following such a policy. Further, we should do everything possible to expand our trade with the free countries of the world. Let us give the fullest consideration to every aspect of this problem. I believe there is a great place for trade missions, for participation in international trade fairs and all those other methods currently being used with such success by our business leaders right here at home in Canada.
If we pursue with determination these two main courses which are yet available to us, the communist economic offensive would run out of steam while, by the same token, all of our economies would be greatly strengthened to the detriment of communism generally.

am at this time going to make a number of remarks about the speech from throne. I should like to say a few things about the remedies which the government is applying in its effort to meet its responsibilities. I should like to outline where in our opinion the real interests of the Canadian people lie, especially in respect of the investment of capital. Before I do this I want to welcome heartily the announcement of the government of its intention to establish a committee of this house to look into the expenditures of the Department of National Defence. On January 12, 1955-that was some five years ago-I had this to say on this matter:
-that a committee of the house be established, or even a royal commission, to investigate all expenditures of the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production since the end of the war. I think the most amazing information would be revealed.
I hope that when this committee is established it will be granted the greatest latitude and authority so that it may do an efficient bit of work. The confidence of the Canadian taxpayer in the defence policy of the government will depend to a large degree on the manner in which this committee will be permitted to do its work and I for one am hoping that the committee will not be merely a rubber stamp for whatever military hierarchy we may have here in Canada.
In reading the speech from the throne it becomes obvious that the government does

When we speak of this prosperity of 1960 -and we read and hear much of it-I think it is our responsibility to consider carefully where this unplanned expansion, this unplanned prosperity, will lead us as a nation. There are already widespread predictions of a major recession such as we have not seen since 1939. These predictions that a major recession will hit us in 1961 or 1962-

I have only 40 minutes and I have about 15 hours of material. If the hon. member would ask his question at the end I shall be obliged.
It is my contention that the force of economic circumstances in the world is going to cause the demise in the '60's of political parties which refuse to realize the role that a national government ought to play in economic matters in modern times. Here we have a major recession widely predicted even by the advisers of the government. A new session of parliament is opening, and yet the government has indicated that it is contemplating no action whatever to protect the Canadian economy. I am afraid that in this as in so many other matters during the past several years the policy will again be one of locking the stable door after the horse is stolen.
We hear much about the prosperity of 1960. Yet a large number of individual Canadians-I believe there are several million of them-are not enjoying a reflection of this prosperity in their present incomes and amenities. I am sure the miners of Nova Scotia do not notice the presence of this prosperity. Canadian agriculture is certainly not enjoying the presence of our so-called prosperity. Our small businessmen who, as private enterprisers, are being squeezed out of existence are certainly not feeling any of the blessings of this prosperity. Our federal civil servants and many other civil servants are certainly not allowed a fair share in this prosperity. And when organized labour approaches management and asks for equity, asks that it also be allowed to share in this prosperity, we find various levels of government imposing anti-labour legislation. May I mention that not only is organized labour in Canada realizing the urgent need to take direct political action, but organized labour also realizes that it must elect a democratic socialist regime if it wants to obtain equity for all; and, wishful thinking notwithstanding, the new political party now being formed will definitely be a socialist party. Organized labour knows it must elect a government devoted to the interests of all sections of our society, and that is the intention of organized labour. There is no use organized labour electing itself a capitalist government. That would be ridiculous.
When we talk about our prosperity we should realize there is no prosperity for the miners of Nova Scotia; there is no prosperity for the farmers, for the small businessmen or for the civil servants. Certainly there is no prosperity for the unemployed, the old

age pensioners or those in receipt of veterans' benefits. This government, by failing to consider measures to ensure a continuation of prosperity or to provide that this prosperity may be shared by all, is to be severely reprimanded and I think the time is not too far distant when it will feel the reaction of the public to its inaction.
May I refer briefly to the subject of foreign trade. In two elections the Prime Minister promised the people of Canada that action would be taken. For several sessions we in this group have called the attention of the government to what was happening in the formation of trading blocks in various parts of the world and especially in Europe. Great possibilities existed there for Canadian participation yet the government sat back and did nothing until the alarm was sounded in Washington. We were asleep at the switch and did not wake up until we observed the interest of the United States in this question. We then sent a couple of cabinet ministers to Washington and, acting like little page boys, they went along with United States officials to make representations overseas. For what purpose?
I contend that it was done in an effort to protect United States interests.
The government ought to realize that we in Canada have our own interests. When making representations in Europe our interests are not identical to nor identifiable with United States interests. We should make our own representations in Europe. We in this group welcome every move that can be made toward the establishment of an Atlantic economic community. However, once again it is a case of arriving at the scene too late. Once more it is a case of attempting to lock the barn door after the horse has been stolen.
I could speak for hours on the question of public financing, tight money and interest rates because I feel it is in this field that the government has most fully revealed the basic Tory philosophy. It is in this area that the government has most harmed the interests of the Canadian people. The government has continued to adhere to discredited monetary theories and to reveal how deeply enslaved it is to the interests of the money lenders of Canada. There seems to be a blind reliance on the value of the money market place, on the part of the government, for the solution of the nation's needs.
One leading economist told me the other day that we have a Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who suffers from monomania in this respect. He can see nothing but the value of the money market place and has no confidence in his ability or that of
The Address-Mr. Regier his government to meet the needs of the country in regard to public financing, tight money and interest rates.
The minister will not agree to use the instruments at hand and under his command. He continues to insist that the Bank of Canada does certain things on its own. He wants to forget that the Bank of Canada Act expressly says that the Minister of Finance on behalf of Canada is the major shareholder of the Bank of Canada. The act also says that the Bank of Canada shall be the fiscal agent of the government. It has been brought out time and time again in the banking and commerce committee of this house that if there is a conflict the will of the government and the minister is to prevail regardless of the opinion of the governor of the Bank of Canada who is, after all, an appointee of the government.
The people of Canada own the Bank of Canada and it is responsible to the government of the day. As a result of what has happened in the past 18 months I feel I can make the prediction that in 1960 tight money will be tighter yet and interest rates will be higher still. Even if the minister is successful in bringing down a balanced budget this year I contend that it will not be enough and that money will be tighter still and interest rates higher yet.
I have analysed the Bank of Canada statistical summary for November last and know exactly the situation in which the minister finds himself in the matter of financing the public debt. Our treasury bills outstanding as of December 2 last were $2,077 million. Bonds and sixth victory loans all due in 1960 total $1,320 million. Ordinarily there are outstanding treasury bills of only $1,495 million. Therefore the minister needs to raise a net amount for servicing the public debt of $1,902 million in order to meet the obligations he will have to meet this year.
Even assuming that he will present a balanced budget and that capital expenditures will be the same as last year,-$400 million- his net bond capital needs run to $2,302 million. Last year he was required to raise only $2,200 million and he failed to raise it. He has a carry-over into this year of $600 million and the situation facing him this year will be worse than that which prevailed last year even if he produces a balanced budget, hence my prediction that tight money will be tighter still and interest rates will be higher yet.
I feel that the minister has been so very wrong in so many predictions he has made in this house as to what the effects of his

The Address-Mr. Regier policies would be that the government, unless it obtains the resignation of that minister, is soon going to find itself in an awful mess.
I should like to read what the minister said as reported at page 2362 of Hansard of July 18, 1958 when he protested that the idea that the bond conversion deal would raise the interest rate was a fallacy:
My hon. friend suggests that this conversion loan is raising interest rates. I do want to make it quite clear that this is not the fact at all.
Later he said:
I am happy to be able to report to the house that the response to the loan already has been not simply encouraging but has indeed been almost overwhelming.
What are the true facts of the situation? The Bank of Canada and the chartered banks had to rescue the minister at the time of the bond conversion deal. Personal holdings of government bonds went down by several hundreds of millions of dollars. If it had not been for the action of the chartered banks and the Bank of Canada the minister's bond conversion deal would have been a flop and would have proved impossible of accomplishment.
The minister and the government through that manoeuvre have caused a loss of public confidence in any issues emanating from the government of Canada. The situation became very desperate. I do not know why, but an interesting event occurred only last August and September. For a seven-week period the minister issued treasury bills yielding in excess of the bank interest rate of 6 per cent. It took seven weeks for him to realize what was happening. I am aware of individual Canadians who took advantage of the situation. I have prepared a table indicating the possible return to an individual who may have obtained a loan of $358 million from a chartered bank depositing as security treasury bills offered by the Minister of Finance. I have a table here in which I have compiled all those issues where the return was in excess of 6 per cent.
An individual who did this, who borrowed the money at the bank, paid the bank 6 per cent, and collected more than 6 per cent from the taxpayers of Canada through the minister, would have made a gross profit of $590,208. I should like to know whether any of those who are closely associated with Conservative party ranks in Canada were aware of the situation. I believe the minister owes the house and the country an explanation of who were the people who were able to obtain from his department the sum of $590,208 as profit without having invested necessarily one cent of their own money.


I regret that seven weeks had elapsed before the Minister of Finance realized what was happening, because he on behalf of the government could have gone to the chartered banks and then the taxpayers would have been responsible for paying only 6 per cent.
In addition the minister has had to resort to excessive and improper use of treasury bills in his predicament. He has raised the amount of treasury bills outstanding in the course of eleven months by over $500 million. He said we had to engage in the conversion loan deal because the market was loaded with short term issues, and it was in order to remove the short term issues from the money markets and thereby make it easier for municipalities and other governments to market their securities that the bond conversion deal was necessary. The minister has now denied that by the fact that after the bond conversion deal was completed it was the actions of the minister himself that flooded the market and we now have the situation where our municipalities and our provincial governments are unable to market their own securities because the offerings of the federal government are clogging the market and the market is badly overloaded with these issues.
The minister has made excessive and wrongful use of treasury bills in Canada and he is not solving anything by so doing. He has, however, completely upset the money market in Canada, thereby gravely injuring the needs or the causes of the municipal and provincial governments. He has also not resolved his own difficulty in that he now has this terrific carryover that he has to deal with in 1960. The money lenders certainly have a good friend in the minister. These are people who sow not but how they can reap when there is a Conservative government in office.
The minister resorts to all sorts of remedies to meet the situation. The government is deliberately encouraging higher and higher interest rates in Canada. The government is deliberately imposing, or permitting the existence of, a tight money situation. The government hbpes it can resolve the situation by asking people to hold the line.
The civil servants of Canada had some dealings with the minister not so long ago. The minister has bluntly refused to this House of Commons the information contained in the civil service commission report in regard to civil servants' salaries. I contend that report is the property of the House of Commons. The civil service commission is an institution which belongs to the House of Commons. The civil servants are not servants of a Tory government. The

civil servants are servants of the people of Canada. At a time when a report like this is issued by a commission responsible to parliament, even though through the Secretary of State-

This Tory government, since they have taken over, in their deliberate policy of paying off the moneylenders, of raising interest rates in Canada, have in effect by now raised interest rates-I am speaking of interest rates in Canada as a whole-by at least 3 per cent. Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada will be interested to know that once this becomes applicable to the whole of the debt of the government of Canada it will mean an added tax burden on the federal government of over $500 million, 3 per cent on its public debt of $17 billion. And when you consider all borrowed money in Canada, when all debts are considered, the people of Canada will have to pay over $1 billion more in added interest rates than they would have paid if the lower interest rates had been permitted to prevail in our economic life in Canada.
The minister says he is not responsible for the tight money policy. The minister, through his actions of raising interest rates has made it uneconomical for Canadian corporations to go to the bond market for their funds. The banks admit that corporation financing in 1959 has to a great degree been done through loans from the chartered banks. That is one of the basic reasons why the small businessman has been unable to borrow money from the chartered banks. As an authority I would like to quote from the Canadian committee report of the investment bankers association of america to their 48th annual convention. They say:
The Address-Mr. Regier A considerable portion of financing in 1959 has been done through the chartered banks instead of the investment dealers.
This report has this to say also.
By refunding 1959 maturities on a short term basis a further amount of about $600 million has been added to 1960 maturities. Hence, the pressure from government refunding issues may well be as great next year as it has been in 1959.
Hence, Mr. Speaker, my prediction that tight money will be tighter still and interest rates will be higher yet unless some action is taken.
The old, discredited policies being pursued in monetary and fiscal matters by this government are going to lead to the recession, widely predicted, becoming not only a recession but a major depression in Canada. We had expected that at least at this session of parliament the government would introduce some measures so that we could make some plans for the continued economic health of the Canadian people.
For instance, we had hoped the government might consider the imposition of a capital gains tax. This would have one salutary effect in that it would make all those people in Canada who earn more than their immediate needs share the tax burden in a more equitable manner than they are doing now. It would have the added beneficial effect of lowering the premium on the Canadian dollar thereby aiding Canadian exporters and Canadian manufacturing enterprises.
But apparently no such action is being contemplated. These higher interest rates add to the tremendous tax burden on our citizens and increase the cost of production in Canada. They also make Canada a happy hunting ground for investors from beyond our borders. Tighter money blocks the sale of provincial and municipal bonds and forces small businessmen out of existence. It blocks the establishment of efficiency in agriculture in Canada.
We need a lot of capital in Canada but the real capital needs of the Canadian people are, for instance, in the Atlantic region. We need a lot of capital for the development of public power. Agriculture can use tremendous amounts of investment capital. Small business can use a lot of it. We need capital to keep the wheels of commerce rolling. Our social needs are being starved for lack of investment capital. Ideally, Canada, for the sake of world peace and world stability, ought to be an exporter of capital rather than an importer.
We definitely feel that the economic anarchy we are allowing to exist must end. The federal government must assume the responsibility for orderly development and the maintenance of a healthy economy. The

The survival and development of the individual human being is the cornerstone of the group to which I belong. We feel that unless action is taken now his survival and development as an individual human being is very much in jeopardy. We say, let us get together and use the instrument of government, the parliament of Canada, in order to advance the cause and the welfare of the general public as a whole.
Some measures were taken in 1934 and again at a later time, and when parliament established the Bank of Canada it assumed authority for the issuance of currency in Canada. We must now move ahead and parliament must assume the responsibility for the issuance of credit in Canada. The Bank of Canada must be given that responsibility. We recommend that one move that should be taken is the establishment of a national investment board which each year would make a survey of the investment needs of all segments of the Canadian economy. It would then make recommendations as to allocation and interest rates with respect to the investment money that is available. When necessary it would recommend legislation which would compel the implementation of such recommendations. If needed because of circumstances it would issue or guarantee bond sales to the public on its own and it would make capital available at an interest rate of not more than 3 per cent for socially desirable projects such as housing and the developmental needs of our municipalities.
We feel that there is growing support throughout Canada for our proposal. We feel that the government is failing the people of Canada at a crucial time in Canadian history and we urge the government to give the most serious consideration to these, to us, necessary actions that they ought to take.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to you for giving me this opportunity to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. My first words will be words of congratulation and good wishes to Your Honour for continued good health so that you may fulfil your duties with the same dignity and devotion that you have displayed during previous sessions. I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) who moved the address in reply


to the speech from the throne. It gave me a great deal of pride and satisfaction that this great honour should be bestowed on him by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). I call the hon. member for Rimouski my good friend. He is not only a master of making good speeches but he is a cheerful neighbour of mine in the chamber. The seconder, the much respected and graceful member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), made a magnificent speech which I am sure will go down in the annals of the house as one of the best.
What I want to speak about today will be a departure from the usual trend of speeches in this chamber. It appears to me that at times we forget that we are sent to parliament as legislators and not only as politicians. At times the speeches made in the house have no relation to legislation or to constructive criticism. They are mostly political speeches that are meant for home consumption. If we can say this about some of the speeches, how much more does it apply to some of the questions that are put to the treasury benches. This, I must say, I detest.
The remarks I intend to make today involve matters of great concern to myself and the people I represent. I am not going to recite the long list of achievements that the government has accomplished during the two and a half years it has been in power. The record is impressive and speaks for itself. Nor will I take hon. members back through the 22 years that the previous government was in power in Canada. My remarks will be in the form of self-criticism or constructive criticism, if you wish to call it that.
During the time that parliament was adjourned a disaster struck the prairie provinces when an unusually early snowfall buried millions of acres of grain. As a result the crop could not be harvested and lies at the present time in the fields. Many farmers were not able to harvest a kernel of grain. Others were able to harvest some. Still others had their grain baled for feed or had to thresh it in a damp condition. The federal government and the provincial governments came to the assistance of the prairie farmers by paying $3 per acre for the unharvested grain but the method of payment of this assistance appears to be unsatisfactory and practically all farmers are complaining about it.
Many farmers did not receive any payment at ali because they took off more than 50 per cent of their crop. This is considered, in many places, unfair. It is my opinion that, to do justice to all, payments should have been made to the farmers on their unharvested crop still in the fields, up to 200 acres, without any strings whatever

attached. This would have been more satisfactory. In addition, the payments should have been started around November 1, the time of the first snowfall. In my opinion, it is still not too late to change this method which would accrue to the advantage of many farmers who will otherwise receive no payment.
Another situation that needs immediate attention is the one concerning deficiency payments on eggs and hogs. The stabilization bill which came into operation a short time ago was met with great enthusiasm and was a success. It is a good piece of legislation but it has some faults. As a result of overproduction, the government had to change the method from purchase by the government to deficiency payments to the producer. The principle of deficiency payments is all right and was approved by the great majority of the producers in this country. However, the method of calculating deficiency payments seems to be working unsatisfactorily.
Under the present set-up deficiency payments will be made to producers on a national average basis which will mean that some producers will receive less than the basic price under the stabilization measure for this year, while others in different parts of the country, by receiving the same amount, will receive much more than the base price guaranteed under the stabilization bill. This, I think, is wrong. I am afraid that if this method is continued we will find to our sorrow that it will make a mockery of our stabilization measure so far as forward pricing is concerned. It will have no resemblance whatever to forward pricing. I am not suggesting the payments should be made on an individual basis, I mean the deficiency payments, which would be difficult to implement, but on a regional basis which would mean many people would receive deficiency payments and these would come very close to the base prices established under the stabilization bill.
This method would apply also to some of the people in our country, namely the butchers and others who are buying pork from the farmer. It appears that the present policy of deficiency payments for pork will have an adverse effect on the butcher shops and the locker plant owners. In rural areas these businessmen buy practically all their pork directly from the farmer. If the price of pork is below the support price then the farmers would not sell to them but would sell to the large packing plants. The only solution would be to have some system set up whereby pork purchased by these small businesses could be graded.
The Address-Mr. Rapp
Serious as these misgivings appear to be, they are only small when compared to the things that face the grain producer in the west. I might sound very critical, Mr. Speaker, but let me tell you I would be failing in my duty if I did not bring these problems of the grain producer in the west to the attention of this house. I was saying that this government had done a tremendous job in alleviating the plight of the farmer. This has been greatly appreciated. The statistics bear out the fact that the farmer's income is up during the last couple of years. I must also say that the grave danger in these statistics lies in generalizing the income of all farmers and this does not present a true picture. Another sad aspect of these farm statistics is the prominence that is given to them in the press and over the radio, thus creating a false impression. A closer look at these figures reveals that the returns from livestock are high, and continue to increase, while the income from grain is low and is steadily declining. The crux of the grain story lies in the disparity of prices.
The income a farmer receives from the sale of grain and the expense he incurs to produce such grain are all out of balance. The gap is simply too great. Of course, this is not a new story that I am revealing to the hon. members in this house. It is almost as old as farming itself in the west. We know also that many factors are contributing to this inequality of income and expenses, but they are too numerous to list at the present time.
What I am interested in is finding ways and means of remedying these inequalities. The only known method, and one proposed by farmers, farm organizations and authorities on agriculture, is a method that will be fair and just to all and in the best interests of Canada's agricultural economy. I refer to the two-price system. This means that the farmer must get one price for the wheat which is used for human consumption and domestic purposes in Canada, and another price for the wheat which he sells on the commercial market or overseas market. This wheat is sold at the world price, whatever that may be.
A similar method of pricing is followed in other industries in this country and is not new. We see it every day. The manufacturer puts his own price on his goods. Industry calculates the price of the finished product on the basis of what it costs to produce, plus labour costs and return on investment. However, the grain producer must accept the price that is offered to him, namely the commercial price offered by our overseas customers which has no relationship whatever to

The Address-Mr. Rapp parity prices. This is the reason for the great disparity between the farmer's income and expenses. The price he receives for wheat remains the same year after year, while the price of farm implements, taxes and other expenses goes up uninterruptedly year after year. For the good of agriculture and our national economy, this must be stopped and the sooner the better.
Actually all the farmers are requesting now is the right and privileges of every other citizen in this country, namely to set a price on his own products when used domestically. The farmer is not asking for a subsidy or that the government should pay the difference between the domestic and the commercial price. He is only asking for parity prices for his wheat used domestically. Our Canadian wheat board would have no difficulty in administering such a scheme since all purchases and sales of western wheat come under their jurisdiction. At the end of every crop year they would have a record of how much wheat had been sold for domestic use and the money so realized would have to be divided amongst the permit holders on the basis of the amount of their wheat which had been sold for domestic use. If a farmer had not sold any wheat at all, he would not be entitled to any extra payments or if he had not sold as much as he was entitled to sell he would get paid only for the amount he sold at the domestic price.
I must say that this is the only solution for the grave situation with which the western grain farmer is faced. It cannot be delayed any longer nor can it be postponed. It might be too late then. The grain farmers look to this government to give them the two-price system because their livelihood depends on grain raising at a price that is fair and just, a parity price for what is used domestically.
I now come to a subject that is very close to my heart and one on which I have spoken in this house on many occasions, namely rapeseed. I am sure Mr. Speaker expects me to say something on this subject. I had not any intention of doing so at the present time but when I discovered that my resolution dealing with this subject is again well down on the list I felt that it was my duty to deal briefly with this matter. 1 was not able to bring forward my resolution last year and the chances for bringing it forward this year are extremely slim also. It is my intention, however, to speak on behalf of the rapeseed producers during this session much more strongly and loudly than ever before, or at least until justice is done for the rapeseed producers.
I am more convinced than ever that the treatment the rapeseed industry is getting

in this country is similar to the treatment a stepchild sometimes receives. Other oilbearing seeds that belong to the same family such as soybeans, sunflower seeds and others are under the stabilization act and are supported by subsidies or deficiency payments, but that is not the situation with regard to rapeseed. I should like to give a short history of the rapeseed industry.
The growing of rapeseed in Canada on a large scale started in 1943. At that time the Canadian navy required marine oil. The Canadian wheat board purchased the rape-seed at that time at six cents per pound, paid all freight charges and so on. But now, after the war, we find that rapeseed is not classified as grain. In the second place, it could not be brought under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. However, when I looked in the statutes of 1952, volume I, chapter 25 I discovered that rapeseed is classified as a grain under the schedules. Acreage in Canada in 1957 was approximately 629,000 acres. Rapeseed ranks as one of the top oil bearing crops in Canada. In terms of world production, Canada has risen from a token producer of rapeseed to the seventh largest producer in the last few years.
Under its present structure freight rates will definitely restrict the development of the rapeseed industry. By way of comparison, wheat, oats, barley and rye and flax all come under the Crowsnest pass agreement while rapeseed does not come under it. For instance, the freight rate on flax is 231 cents per hundredweight while that on rapeseed is closer to 80 cents. Consequently rapeseed is subjected to further increase in freight rates as they become effective as it does not come under the Crowsnest pass agreement.
Handling, marketing and storage of rape-seed is identical to that with respect to other grains. Rapeseed is accepted and carried by ocean carriers at the same rate for transportation as flax or other grains. The only people who seemingly do not recognize rape-seed as a grain are the Canadian railways. So far as the railroads are concerned, they have the same costs in handling rapeseed as in handling other grains. Canadian railways recognized that rapeseed was identical with flax so far as they are concerned, recognizing for the purpose of transportation there is no difference between flax and rapeseed.
In addition to the question of freight rates, tariffs have also affected the expansion of this industry. Rapeseed, when processed, is manufactured into an edible oil comparable to soybean oil, cottonseed oil, or any of the other oils on the vegetable oil market. A byproduct of processing rapeseed is the meal

which is used in this country in the production of livestock and poultry feeds and concentrates. At the present time our tariff structure allows soybean oil, the largest competitor to rapeseed oil, into Canada from the United States under a 20 per cent tariff. However, soybeans are brought in duty free; processed here and the oil can be sold on the Canadian market. The Canadian processor may also ship the oil back into the United States without tariffs or without duty while Canadian rapeseed taken into the United States must pay one cent per pound import tax.
My interest in this question is precipitated by the following reasons which I list under these five points:
1.	Wheat acreage reduction is essential to reducing our present surplus stock. Diversifying production is essential and rapeseed is a cash crop that can be grown as an alternative to wheat.
2.	Production of soybeans is rapidly expanding in the cornbelt of the United States. The United States government is depressing the world market with cheap flax and soybeans. Faced with this unfair competition in world markets, surely our government can protect our producers by putting our product in a competitive position on our home market.
3.	The vegetable oil market in Canada is expanding. It has been estimated that there would be a ready market for a million acres of rapeseed annually if action is taken on freight rates and tariffs to place it in a competitive position with oil seed products we presently import from the United States.
4.	Rapeseed is the only edible oil seed at present that can be produced in sufficient quantities to meet our Canadian demand for edible oil under normal peacetime conditions, and marine engine oil in the event of war. Growing of other edible oil-bearing seeds is restricted by climatic conditions.
5.	There is room for a gradual expansion of our livestock industry in Canada. Rape-seed meal as a high protein concentrate has proven suitable for preparation of livestock and poultry feeds and concentrates.
With this, Mr. Speaker, I will conclude my critical analysis. As I stated at the outset, the government has done a tremendous job with regard to legislation pertaining to agriculture, and I am sure it will continue to do so in the future. Much of the legislation pertaining to agriculture has been new legislation that has never been in operation previously. In other words it has been put into effect on a trial and error basis. It is expected that, as time goes on, changes and amendments will be required. However, the subjects I have listed in my speech are
The Address-Mr. Dupuis unquestionably the most important ones, and require the immediate and considerate attention of our government. The farmers are depending on this, and it has been my duty and pleasure to speak on their behalf. (Translation):

Well, I ask him now, since he does not live far from the district where the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean is established, to take steps that the present government may fulfil the promise of the previous government to set up at the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean a complete educational course for officer-cadets.
Allow me to point out, Mr. Speaker, that French-speaking cadets of the College de Saint-Jean find themselves handicapped when they have to go to Kingston to complete their studies where only English is spoken. It is not because French people cannot speak English, but when a Frenchspeaking cadet is transferred to exclusively English surroundings, he necessarily leaves behind a very favourable situation at the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean and is thereby out of his element in a college where only English is spoken.
Mr. Speaker, I ask once again and for the third time that French-speaking cadets, as well as English-speaking cadets who may wish to, be given the opportunity to take the complete officers' course at the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean, since we are in a position to enable them to do so.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the house that we are looking forward not only to the speech of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, but also to those of his colleagues.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising on the address in reply to the speech from the throne my first words must be of congratulations to you that we see you again in the chair in such good health and spirits and certainly, sir, I am glad to see that the recess has not at all dulled your great sense of wit. You come back to this house again as perhaps the wittiest man here, with a wit that is used on occasions where it is more important than at any other time.
I would also like to express my congratulations to the new Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees, and also, again to you, sir, in that your assistant is a man who is so able and so well qualified. I have noted that members everywhere in the house agree that the Deputy Speaker is as good a man as could be appointed to that position from the ranks of the house.
The Address-Mr. MacLellan
Also, I wish to express my congratulations to the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Mor-issette) who made such an excellent speech in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I listened carefully to his speech, and I read it again in Hansard. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I think nothing illustrates more clearly the work that has been done by this government in fostering the nation, indeed how much more the Canadian citizen generally is now getting for his tax money, than the illustrations of the hon. member for Rimouski in his very excellent speech at the opening of this debate. He pointed out that in the year 1956-1957, the per capita tax paid to the federal government in Canada amounted to $321.14. In the form of social benefits the sum returned to the taxpayer in the same year, the last year of Liberal administration, amounted to $86 per person. Only two years later, 1958-1959, we find that the per capita taxes paid in Canada have decreased to $271.16 per person, while at the same time the social security benefits have increased across the nation to $120 per person per year or, as the hon. member pointed out, an increase of 39.5 per cent in social security payments over the last years of the Liberal administration.
I would also like to express my congratulations to the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) who with such poise and eloquence delivered a very warm speech on that same afternoon. She also illustrated how Canada has been expanding, and what growth we have seen, under the administration of the present government.
I would like to add my felicitations to those of other members to the two new cabinet ministers whom we have seen appointed since the house last sat, and to all of the parliamentary secretaries, in particular to my very good friend, the parliamentary secretary to the Postmaster General. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris) is very highly regarded and well liked by all of the members from Nova Scotia, and indeed by all members in this house, and his appointment was widely welcomed and commended by all of the people of Nova Scotia. His appointment is well received everywhere in our province. From my knowledge of the secretary and my acquaintance with his capability for work I am certain that he will make a significant contribution to the progress of Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, one of the things I noticed in the speech of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) today, and it is a comment that is quite familiar in the house in these days, was his reference to the number of people who draw unemployment insurance benefits in his riding. He says there

The Address-Mr. Machellan are some five thousand who at the moment are drawing unemployment insurance in Gloucester and he regards this as a terrible thing, a disgrace. Mr. Speaker, there can be nothing more hypocritical than that. There are many areas in Canada where without question there is going to be seasonal unemployment. In ridings like that of the hon. member for Gloucester, and in my riding, almost 80 per cent of the working force is unable to earn wages in the wintertime simply because the weather prohibits it.
Many of my constituents, like his, are fishermen. They certainly do not fish in the wintertime. Many of our people work on construction projects. They cannot carry on that trade to the same extent in the wintertime despite every effort made by the government to provide special winter work. What it amounts to after all is that these people who have worked in the summertime have qualified for unemployment benefits which they need in the winter. They have always needed unemployment benefits in the winter. If they did not draw them to the same extent before, Mr. Speaker, it was only because there was not the work available in the summertime to allow them to qualify for insurance benefits in the wintertime.
As far as the people of my riding are concerned, the more seasonally employed people there are who draw benefits in the wintertime the better it suits me, and if I congratulate this government on one thing more than anything else it is the fact that the tremendous construction program of the last two years in harbour facilities and public buildings, has meant a substantial increase in employment in the summertime, which has also meant that more people have qualified for benefits in the wintertime. The number of people drawing unemployment insurance benefits in Atlantic coast ridings in the wintertime is the barometer of prosperity in the summer, and the more the better.
While I am on this topic, I notice that perhaps as a result of the effort to conquer the seasonal unemployment problem the government is making quite an attempt to spur the winter works program and tending to put off until winter much of what could be done in the summer. That is all very well but I would urge the government, where there are men looking for work in the summer, to be careful not to postpone to the wintertime work that could be done better in warmer weather. In the case of the construction of wharves, breakwaters and similar works in my constituency, I would prefer that projects not be put off until winter when they could be done better in the summer.

Despite the protestations of the opposition that the number of people drawing unemployment insurance is something to be ashamed of, I would suggest that we are always going to have a certain amount of seasonal unemployment and we have got to accept it. It will always apply to a certain percentage of our working force, and as long as these people are getting unemployment insurance benefits the situation should not be thrown at the government and the people of Canada as something we should be ashamed of. We have to accept that situation. It is a mistake to put off until wintertime work that could be better done in the summer provided there are men seeking work in summer or fall.
Another point in the hon. member's speech that drew my attention was his reference to the deficits of the last two years. Other members in the opposition have made similar references, particularly the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) in his rather astounding speech this afternoon when he cried loud and long about the deficits of the last two years. It seems to me that the people who make the most noise in asking for expenditures are the people who then come along to bewail the fact that taxes have to be raised to pay for these expenditures or that in some situations deficits may be incurred.
In 1957-58 we suffered a recession and there was an urgent need for extraordinary spending on public works. That expenditure meant a lot in my riding and I am sure in the ridings of every other member of the house. The money to pay for it could not come out of the air. If it could not be raised by taxation in that particular year then there had to be a deficit. Nothing is more nonsensical than continual requests for greater public expenditures and at the same time violent protestations about the fact that these projects have to be paid for.
I must say that the same thing applies to interest rates. During the session last year every member in the house was asking the government to encourage housing, to go into the market and borrow money so that it could be made available to people to build badly needed homes. Every member, including members like the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, wanted the government to spend every possible cent it could find to relieve the unemployment situation. No matter what project was suggested, the C.C.F. group called it "peanuts". There always had to be more money. Surely they should be the last to complain about a deficit brought about by the provision of employment for people who badly needed it during the recession, and by the same token they should be the last to
[Mr. MacLellan.l

complain about the interest that must be paid on public borrowings to meet necessary public expenditures to provide employment.
It is so easy to live in a fairyland. It is suggested that the government is responsible for interest rates. I have never seen a situation yet where interest rates were set by the borrower. They are set by the lender. The government is a borrower just the same as any other person or agency in the Dominion of Canada. It borrows as cheaply as it can and the rate is always set by the man in the street whose savings provide the money to purchase the bonds of the nation. There is no other source of money. It is so easy to rise in this house and say that the interest rate on housing loans should be 6 per cent or less, but the simple fact is that unless the interest rate were raised on National Housing Act loans the money that is needed for housing would not be diverted by the people of Canada into housing.
This money does not come from the government but from the people and they will only lend it when they feel they are getting an interest rate that is in line with the interest rate they could get from other investments. If we want money for housing we must be prepared to pay the market interest rate for it. Nobody likes to pay interest. How wonderful it would be if the interest rate could be 2 per cent on every government bond. But when bonds of first class mortgage and other corporations bearing interest of five and a half to six and a half per cent are available in the market, how can any government borrow long term money for housing at a rate of less? The simple fact is that we cannot borrow money unless we make the interest rate attractive to the lender.
At the same time that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam blamed the government for high interest rates he also referred to the conversion loan. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, what the situation would be if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) were going forth into the Canadian money market now to raise money to refinance the war debt. There is no mystery about the conversion loan. During the war we, necessarily, put a mortgage on the country to pay for weapons and to keep men in the field overseas. That debt was coming due in 1959, 1960 and 1961. There were only two things that could be done; we could either refinance or default. The interest rate paid in the conversion loan was not set by the Minister of Finance. It was the best interest rate he could obtain in the market and neither he nor anybody else in this house could do anything about it. We were lucky to get the money at that price.
Having in mind the condition of the money market at that time and the fact that other
The Address-Mr. MacLellan first-class bonds with an interest rate of 5 or 5i per cent were available on the market, I must say that the Minister of Finance certainly pulled a hat trick in refinancing the war loans in the manner that he did. Imagine the situation if instead of asking people to convert the bonds they held into new bonds the old bonds had been allowed to fall due, as some members suggest should have been done, and then we would have to go piecemeal into the market after the money. The Minister of Finance would have had a much poorer chance to get the money at a decent rate than was the case when he moved as he did. One of the greatest steps that has been taken by this government was to refinance our war loans at what we all know to be a reasonable rate of interest in terms of what money cost on the market at the time.
There is another thing that bothered the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in his fairyland speech. It is the fact that on some occasions the government has had to pay over 6 per cent on treasury bills. Again I say that the government does not set the interest rate on treasury bills. The rate is set by the lenders, it is set by the market, and if the Minister of Finance cannot put out treasury bills at 6 per cent when he needs short term money then he has to raise the interest rate to get the money. What sense is there in saying that he can get the money from the banks? The banks are like any other buyer. They will buy investments in the best market and at the best price they can get.

speechtext: Who got the rake-off?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The rake-off, if there was any rake-off, went to the people of Canada who provided the money. Where does the money come from? The banks get their money from the man on the street who deposits it with them. They pay interest on his deposit. Otherwise they do not get the money. A mortgage company or other lender does not manufacture money out of the air. It borrows it from the average citizen who has to be paid a certain interest rate or he will not make money available to the mortgage company.
