If the hon. member has no objection, I would prefer to answer his question after I have finished. Someone has suggested, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) I believe, that the answer is for the Bank of Canada to print money. There is no easier answer to the problem of high cost money than to print money.

The Address-Mr. MacLellan The difficulty is that suddenly the people who own bonds and people who receive pensions find that prices go up and they cannot afford to buy the things they need. Nothing could be simpler for rampant inflation.
But the most astounding thing I heard this afternoon, in fact one of the most astonishing things I have heard since entering this house was the proposal by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that a board of investment should be established to make money available to the provinces-he referred to the Atlantic provinces and we thank him for that-and to municipalities at 3 per cent. Where is such a board of investment going to get money to lend at 3 per cent? Money does not grow on trees. It has to be borrowed in the market or raised by taxes. If such a board of investment were to go into the market like the government does where would it be able to raise money at 3 per cent to lend to somebody else? I certainly wonder sometimes how members of the opposition can keep their household accounts straight when they know no better than to think that the money needed by the government of Canada can be borrowed by the waving of a wand. Perhaps they think that suddenly a miracle will occur to allow the government of Canada to borrow money at half the cost the money markets demand for it.
Now, in the present situation, where we have a danger of inflation, it is incumbent upon the government, whether or not it likes it, to make as much money available for the expansion of industry in the nation as possible, and also to aid in providing a cheaper money market by cutting down its own expenditures wherever it can. At the moment, as hon. members have mentioned, there seems to be a definite intention to cut government expenditures wherever possible so that the money thereby saved will be available to other agencies and persons in the nation who require it. While that is being done, I would urge upon the government that it be careful of the priority of expenditure cuts and to ensure that a large percentage of the money the government is spending is spent on productive capacity, to build facilities that must be used to earn income. These should be the last expenditures to be cut.
The difference, for example, can be illustrated by mentioning harbour facilities which are used in my riding by fishermen to provide a product which they can sell, and the building of a post office or a building of that nature which, in itself, does not produce anything. If some expenditures have to be put off at the present time I would urge that, as


much as possible, income producing expenditures be maintained. I might also say that the fishing industry of the province of Nova Scotia, which earns around $50 million a year, is a great earner of foreign exchange. Most of our fish is sold below the border in the United States. Wherever fish is caught and sold it helps to meet the problem of our trade deficit.
Everyone realizes that with the money situation as it is in Canada we need all the foreign capital we can get. It was suggested this afternoon that high interest rates are attracting foreign capital and that that is a disgraceful situation. One of our present financial problems is that foreign capital finds an attractive market at home. American capital particularly is not as ready as formerly to buy Canadian bonds. We are great importers of capital. We have to be to maintain the standard of expansion we want in this country. We can acquire capital in only two ways; one by saving, and the other by borrowing. We have to do both as best we can in the years ahead to meet the problems that we will meet in the monetary field.
Now, speaking particularly of my own riding, and speaking again of income producing expenditures, I should like to compliment the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) for the tremendous boost he has given the tourist industry in my province, during the short time he has been in office. A large section of Cape Breton Highlands national park lies in Inverness county. During the last two years there has been a tremendous construction program going on in the park, the paving of roads, the building of campsites and the laying out of tourist accommodation. I call this an income producing expenditure.
I should like to point out that in visitors to the Cape Breton Highlands national park there was an increase of 34,541 people, or 20 per cent, in 1958. In 1959 there were over 189,000 people who registered at Cape Breton Highlands national park, an increase of 50 per cent over 1957. The great percentage of these people were tourists from the United States and they spent a great deal of money in Nova Scotia. The tourist industry itself in Cape Breton island increased by 17 per cent in 1959 and 39 per cent the year before. This increase results in more expenditure by United States citizens not only in my constituency and province but in Canada. It is a wise Canadian investment, to develop tourist facilities and to invest money to increase our tourist industry. I should like to compliment the minister again upon how well the work is being done in Cape Breton Highlands national park and how fruitful it has

been. Employment has been provided in one section of my riding and this has provided a very prosperous summer. More important, however, is the development of the tourist industry. There is hardly a town or village throughout the province in which there is not a substantial and profitable tourist investment. Probably the biggest single investment in many of our small towns is in tourist motels and hotels.
I urgently suggest that the minister should carry on with the development of our national parks. Within two days' drive of Nova Scotia lies the tremendous population of the northeastern United States. This population is jammed into crowded cities and looks forward to relief from the heat along the seashores of Canada in the summertime. We should welcome these people and do everything we can to develop this industry. Tourism is unlimited and is one of the great present and potential industries not only of Nova Scotia but indeed of Canada. Money spent by the government for national parks to provide better facilities and make tourists welcome is an investment that will pay us well in the years ahead. Very few expenditures by the government actually pay greater dividends in the form of happiness and recreation for our people as well as contributing to actual earnings.
I was also pleased to see announced the agreement between Nova Scotia and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in regard to the roads to resources program. This will provide some $15 million, in combination with the province, for the building of roads into tourist areas. I am particularly pleased to see that the program provides for the building of a road in my riding from Grand Anse through West Bay and Marble Mountain. This road will open up some of the most beautiful scenery in Nova Scotia and allow tourists in to see these peaceful lands which I am sure were made to provide relief from the problems these people have as a result of living in hot and crowded cities.
I should also like again to draw the attention of the minister to the fortress of Louis-bourg. I may say when I first came to Ottawa I was rather shocked at how little interest there was to be found in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the fortress of Louisbourg. After my conversations with the minister and others in his department I am very pleased to see the interest they are taking in the development of this historic fortress. Last summer we had the services of a very prominent and skilled archaeologist who did a lot of
The Address-Mr. MacLellan the planning work necessary for the development of the Louisbourg historic site.
Louisbourg is one of the most important monuments in Canadian history. It was once one of the greatest fortresses in the world. It cost France so much in the days of Louis XIV that every morning he came to the window of his palace to see if he could see the spires of Louisbourg rising in the western sky. Unfortunately, after 1758 the fortress was destroyed at the request of the New England colonies who did not want this stronghold overlooking the gulf of St. Lawrence and the fishing grounds of the north Atlantic.
It should be remembered that the work that has been done there to date has been only a start, and there will be much more money needed to restore this fortress. However, the expenditures made in developing Louisbourg will be an investment, not only in restoring one of Canada's greatest monuments but also one which will pay good dividends in tourism to the people of Nova Scotia.
Interest in Louisbourg fortress is as widespread as in any other historical monument on this continent. It is not only a great Canadian memory but it also contains a chapter of the history of the people of the New England states, many of whose ancestors died in battles outside the walls of the fort. The other day I was talking to a prominent Canadian executive who came originally, I believe, from Massachusetts. When he learned I was a Nova Scotian, the first question he asked me was this: "What is being done about the development of Louisbourg?" He said, "There is great interest in this fortress in my own state and generally in New England and many people there are interested in seeing Louisbourg developed."
From the tourist point of view, the island of Cape Breton has a great attraction in the national park in the north. To round out our tourist economy there should be an important tourist attraction in the southwestern part of the island. The natural attraction would be Louisbourg. Something more should be done to show our visitors from the United States and from the other provinces just what we have in this historic spot. I noticed a great increase in 1958-59 in the attendance at the fortress in Louisbourg. Twenty five per cent more people called at Louisbourg to walk over the fortress grounds and to review there that phase of the history of Canada in 1958-59 than in 1957-58. I would again recommend to the minister that planning and expenditures for the fortress of Louisbourg are important not only as a matter of preserving Canadian history, but also as a boost to the tourist industry in Nova Scotia.

The Address-Mr. MacLellan
I was very pleased to note in the throne speech that a department of forestry will be established in the federal government. More and more Canada's forests are becoming valuable as the demand for paper and other forest products increases. At the moment plans have been laid and construction is soon to begin on a $40 million pulp mill in my riding at Point Tupper to utilize the great timber resources in eastern Nova Scotia. While I say "great timber resources", at the same time we all know that those timber resources are limited and that unless they are used properly and unless there is proper conservation there is a risk that we shall be unable to supply to this mill sufficient raw material across the years ahead. The establishment of a department of forestry at this particular time in Canada is an extremely important step towards marshalling our forest resources and establishing a proper conservation program. I know that the people of my riding are very willing to co-operate with federal and provincial authorities in setting up a conservation program which will assure that Nova Scotia Pulp Limited and its new mill at Point Tupper will have for generations to come the raw material it requires.
I also should like to take a moment to express to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the government our satisfaction at, and our thanks for the appointment of a commission to examine into the Nova Scotia coal problem. I suppose no problem in Canada is more beset by inaccuracies, rumours and misunderstandings than is our important coal industry. I am glad to see that a brilliant jurist is to go into the problem with the perspective of a jurist and to come forth with the answers to many questions that people are asking.
Indeed there are many questions that will be put before him. He must decide, for example, whether the selling of natural gas at prices below cost in order to encourage present coal users in the province of Quebec to switch to natural gas is fair competition or is in restraint of trade. He must decide whether natural gas, which after all is a resource of only 25 years' proven potential in Canada should be used for production of industrial energy when coal could be more profitably used in terms of the preservation of natural gas and similar fuels for domestic household use and similar utilizations of energy.
He has many questions to decide but, I think more important than anything else, if he can help to show to the people of Canada that the Nova Scotia coal problem is not simply a social problem, is not simply
a matter of providing employment for miners in Nova Scotia, but is an important Canadian economic problem, he will have done a great favour not only to Nova Scotia but indeed to the people of Canada.
Some Canadians have been caught up with the idea that oil and gas are Canada's great energy resources when as a matter of fact the principal energy resource in Canada is coal. It constitutes 90 per cent of the energy in Canada. Oil and gas combined provide only 10 per cent of the potential energy resources of Canada.
It has been suggested for example that by 1970 the province of Ontario will require to produce electricity the energy that is created by 10 million tons of coal a year, more than twice our present production in Nova Scotia. Canadians must realize that the coal industry must be kept alive in order to provide the energy that will be needed in the future. At the same time they must realize that fuels like oil and gas are actually very limited in extent. Their potential is very small and they must be conserved in order to provide a type of energy, such as that for engines and motors, which cannot be provided by coal.
I have said before that there is probably more confusion about the nature of the problem of the Nova Scotia coal industry than there is about any other problem in Canada.
It seems that everyone who speaks or writes on the subject has a different idea. For example, it is common for writers on the coal industry and for those who would assist coal to suggest that tariffs should be provided in order to shut out United States coal. As a matter of fact, United States coal is not a serious competitor of Nova Scotia coal. We can now sell as cheaply in some cases as can the Americans in the province of Ontario under the present subvention and we can sell much more cheaply in the province of Quebec.
